The October 30, 2019 FOMC statement signals an accommodative shift: a 25 bp cut to 1.50–1.75% and renewed T-bill purchases and repo operations to maintain ample reserves. Empirical and structural evidence suggests this easing should support real activity. Sims’ money-and-output results indicate monetary policy shocks propagate to real output in the short run, and Christiano–Eichenbaum show that with nominal rigidities, easier policy raises labor hours—consistent with the Committee’s observation of “solid” job gains and low unemployment. With inflation and survey-based expectations below 2%, the decision aligns with Svensson’s emphasis on forecast-based inflation targeting and reinforces credibility lessons drawn from the Volcker era about responding to deviations from target. Offsetting this, weak business fixed investment and exports, plus global uncertainties, temper the outlook. Net effect: a cautiously positive stance, with the literature implying the easing should cushion downside risks and modestly lift growth and employment toward objectives.
